en.g: Molde (the administrative centre, city, and municipality of Møre og Romsdal, Western Norway, Norway)

1000761.etyen:
Originally the name of a farmstead, from Old Norse Moldar, the plural form of either mold (“earth, dirt, soil”), or moldr (“skull, mould”) in reference to the rounded peaks in Moldemarka.
In the 18th century and later, the name Moldegaard was used about the farm.

en.g: Used to form female given names, especially from male given names and, less commonly, from other female given names; a less common variant of -ine

1001017.etyen:
A less common variant of -ine (“female name-forming suffix”). The Norwegian name-forming pattern was transmitted through Danish from German and ultimately reflects Latin -īna (“feminine form of -īnus”), the feminine of -īnus (“of or pertaining to”). Names in -ina formed part of the same naming fashion as the more widespread formations in -ine.
Compare Danish -ina and Swedish -ina (“female name-forming suffix”).

en.g: a female given name from Latin [in turn from Koine Greek, in turn from Biblical Hebrew], equivalent to English Jane, traditionally regarded as the feminine counterpart of Johannes

1001273.etyen:
A younger form of Johanna, ultimately from Latin Iōhanna, a variant of Joanna, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννα (Iōánna), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָה (Yôḥānāh, “Yahweh is gracious”). The Hebrew name is the feminine form corresponding to יְהוֹחָנָן (Yəhōḥānān), the source of Johannes. First attested in the 15th century in Norway.
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk Johanne, Danish Johanne, Swedish Johanne, Icelandic Jóhanna, Faroese Jóhanna, German Johanna, English Joanna and French Johanne (“female given name”).

en.g: a female given name from Old Norse Áshildr [in turn from Proto-Germanic], variant of Åshild
x: Aashild kommer på besøk i morgen.
Aashild is coming to visit tomorrow.
«Søn til fru Aashild!» sa Kristin storundrende.
“Lady Aashild's son!” Kristin said in great astonishment.

1001785.etyen:
PIE word
 *h₂émsus
Variant of Åshild, retaining the traditional spelling ⟨aa⟩ for ⟨å⟩.
Ultimately from Old Norse Áshildr, from Proto-Germanic *Ansuhildiz, equivalent to áss (“god; one of the Æsir”) + hildr (“battle”), literally “god-battle”.
The first element is from Proto-Germanic *ansuz (“god”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂émsus, itself from the root *h₂ems- (“to engender, beget”). The second element is from Proto-Germanic *hildiz (“battle, fight”); its deeper origin is uncertain, though derivation from Proto-Indo-European *kelh₂- (“to hit, strike”) has been proposed.

1004345.etyen:
A variant spelling of Jul m. The exact origin may differ between bearers. Norwegian name literature analyses Jul as:
# a dialectal variant of Gjul, ultimately from Old Norse Gjurðr m;
# a short form of Julius; or
# a continuation of Old Danish Jul, a younger form of Old Norse Ígull m, from ígull (“sea urchin, hedgehog”).
Compare Danish Juul and Swedish Juul (“male given name”).

a surname from habitational, from a farm named Trygstad or a related farm name

1004601.etyen:
From an Old Norse farm name of the Þrygstaðir type. The first element is uncertain; the second is staðir (“farms, homesteads”), the plural of staðr (“place, farmstead”). The surname is habitational, from a farm bearing this name.
Compare Trøgstad, another modern outcome of the same place-name type.

en.g: SSS islands; a group of islands in the Caribbean, comprising Saba, Sint Eustatius and Sint Maarten, in the northern Lesser Antilles
x: SSS-øyene ligger nordøst i Karibia, langt fra ABC-øyene.
The SSS islands lie in the northeastern Caribbean, far from the ABC islands.
SSS-øyene består av Sint Maarten, Saba og Sint Eustatius, som ligger øst for Puerto Rico.
The SSS islands consist of Sint Maarten, Saba and Sint Eustatius, which lie east of Puerto Rico.

1004857.etyen:
Probably a calque of Dutch SSS-eilanden (“SSS islands”). The initialism is formed from the names of the three islands: Dutch Saba (S), Sint Eustatius (S) and Sint Maarten (S).
The final element, øyene (“the islands”), is the definite plural of øy (“island”), inherited from Old Norse ey (“island”), from Proto-Germanic *awjō (“island, floodplain”), from earlier *agwjō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ékʷeh₂ (“water”).
Parallel formations include Dutch SSS-eilanden, German SSS-Inseln, French îles SSS, Spanish islas SSS and English SSS islands (“SSS islands”).

en.g: a mild oath, expletive, or exclamation, roughly damn or wow, used to express disgust, irritation, surprise, admiration, or another strong reaction
x: Fyttegrisen, så fort den bilen kjørte!
Damn, that car was going fast!
fytte grisen så forbanna fattern blei

1005113.etyen:
Contraction of fy (“fie, shame”) + til (“to”) + grisen (“the pig”), literally “fie to the pig”.
The first element, fy (“fie, shame”), is imitative, originally representing a spitting sound. The final element is the definite singular of gris (“pig”), Inherited from Old Norse gríss (“pig, boar”), which has been connected with Proto-Germanic *grīsaną (“to shudder, be frightened”); the further origin of the Proto-Germanic word is disputed.
